title: Learning by heart
hookLine: lines learned by heart go where books can't: at the first council, Ananda recited the Buddha's teachings from memory, "thus have I heard"
tomorrow: an emperor kept a notebook nobody was meant to read. why?

cards: Phone dead, no signal, and the one number still remembered is a parent's landline from childhood. Some things stay where batteries don't reach.

After the Buddha died, tradition says, his teachings weren't written in any book. They lived in people. So, the Vinaya texts say, the senior monk Kassapa called the elders together at Rajagaha to say it all back.
And they needed one man in particular: Ananda, the Buddha's attendant, who had heard him teach again and again.

teach.h: BEFORE HIS HEAD REACHED THE PILLOW.

teach.b: Ananda wasn't yet fully awakened, and the elders around him were. The night before, the story goes, he sat up practicing, and as he finally lay down to rest, before his head reached the pillow, he woke up all the way.
The next day Kassapa questioned him in front of the assembly. Where was this teaching given? To whom?
About what? And Ananda answered, teaching after teaching, from memory.
Tradition says that's why the suttas open in Ananda's voice: "Thus have I heard." Evam me sutam.
The Buddhist teaching inside it: the Dharma was kept by heart and said together, voice to voice, and Buddhists still chant the old texts aloud.
A line learned by heart goes where books can't: into a hospital room, a sleepless night, a child's bedroom with the lights off. For your own study, that's the practice.
Choose one line worth carrying, and carry it the way Ananda did.

how: Tradition hears Ananda in the suttas' opening words, "thus have I heard", and Buddhists chant the old texts aloud together. People on many paths learn a few lines by heart to carry through the day.

o: reading a book so fast you remember only the outline
copying a passage by hand to hang on the wall
keeping a line inside you so it goes where books can't

games.q: a friend wants to keep one teaching close during a hard hospital stay, where reading is hard. by Ananda's story, what fits?
o: learn one short line by heart now, so it's there when no book is.
bring the thickest book she owns and read it cover to cover.
skip it; teachings only count when you read them from the page.
games.why: Ananda carried the teachings in memory to the council. A line learned by heart goes where books can't.

practice: Choose one short line you'd like to keep, from your book or from this week. Say it out loud slowly, three times, then once more with your eyes resting on nothing. For the rest of the sit, let it repeat quietly inside, like a chant.
